scenes.heading: Tone, language and persuasion
scenes.sub: How writers sound, and how they change your mind
scenes.say: Writers don't just tell you things. They choose every word to make you feel something. These questions check whether you can hear the writer's voice and spot their tricks.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: 'Nice one' can sound kind or cutting, by tone of voice
scenes.science: On paper, word choice and punctuation create the tone
scenes.breaks: on paper you can't hear a voice, so you must read the loaded words and the situation.
scenes.say: Say nice one in a warm voice, then in a cutting voice. Same words, different meaning. That's tone. On paper you can't hear a voice, so you read the loaded words, the punctuation and the situation instead.

scenes.heading: Persuasive techniques
scenes.say: Learn the big persuasive techniques. Emotive language stirs feelings. Rhetorical questions make the answer seem obvious. Inclusive language puts you on the writer's side. Statistics and experts make it seem reliable. And watch for anecdotes, repetition and exaggeration.

scenes.heading: Simile or metaphor?

right.title: Metaphor
points: The library was the jewel of the street

scenes.say: Don't mix up similes and metaphors. A simile compares using like or as: snores like distant thunder. A metaphor says one thing is another: the library was the jewel of the street.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: 'Brilliant planning — the only drinking tap is behind a locked door.' What is the tone?
scenes.say: Brilliant planning, the only drinking tap is behind a locked door. Brilliant is a nice word, but the situation is bad. Nice words plus a nasty situation means sarcasm.

scenes.heading: Answering technique questions
steps: Say its effect on the reader
scenes.say: For technique questions, find the loaded words, name the technique, then say its effect: the writer uses it to make the reader feel or do something. And always check the situation for irony.

points: Tone = tone of voice on paper
scenes.say: Quick recap. Tone is a tone of voice on paper. Connotation explains why writers pick cosy instead of cramped. Always link a technique to its effect. And the side with the most emotive language is usually the writer's side. Now try the practice questions!
